summary: Monongahela NF fire tower named for ranger Donald Gaudineer; built 1936-37 by CCC crews, in service to the early 1970s; only concrete footings and a trailhead plaque remain.

facts.status_note: Only concrete footings remain, per the registry and Wikipedia.

access.note: On Monongahela National Forest land with drive-up access via FR 27A. A plaque at the trail start sits feet from the tower's foundation, per Mon Forest Towns.

visit.trail_note: Easy half-mile Gaudineer Loop through mossy second-growth spruce in the Gaudineer Scenic Area, per Mon Forest Towns.

events.note: Registry gives 1936 as the build year; construction ran 1936-1937 by CCC crews working from Camp Hutton.
Wikipedia says the tower surveyed the forest from 1936. The registry and e-WV tie construction to 1936-37 and the dedication to 1937, so the start is disputed.
Dedicated July 5, 1937 in memory of Ranger Donald R. Gaudineer.
Early 1970s per e-WV; the registry says it remained in service until the early 1970s. Recorded as 1970 for the early 1970s.
Registered September 16, 2008 with the Former Fire Lookout Sites register.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikipedia gives April 27, 1936 and e-WV gives April 28, 1936. The story says April 1936, which both sources support.

The registry lists Randolph County and the Forest Lookouts header lists Pocahontas County. The county list shows Pocahontas. Wikipedia places the knob on the Randolph / Pocahontas line, which the story uses.

Wikipedia says the tower surveyed the forest from 1936 through the 1970s. The registry and e-WV date the build to 1936-37 and the dedication to 1937. The story gives the 1937 dedication and says the sources disagree.
e-WV places the dedication on Cheat Mountain, while Wikipedia describes the knob as the highest point of Shavers Mountain. The story does not name a mountain.

sources.title: Walking the Old Watch: Former Fire Tower Hikes in the Monongahela

notes_for_editor: Brief record fits the sources: gone, U.S. Forest Service, built 1936, registered 2008. Gaudineer's death date differs by one day across sources (April 27 vs 28, 1936), so the story says April 1936. The registry and Wikipedia disagree on when the tower began watching the forest. Tower height and design are not stated in any fetched source and are omitted. No staffing, fire, or rental records were found. Photo credits (May 2016 footings photo, Brian Powell; 1947 H. C. Frayer photo, National Archives) were noted but no image URLs were captured, so no photos are listed. A search snippet said a 1941 visitor saw the tower standing and that it was dismantled later; neither claim was on a page I could read, so neither is used.
